corpus.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
corpus.signal_text:
Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.
“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.
He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.
On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.
Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.
“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.
“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.
Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.
Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.
However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

corpus.title: Serbia's president criticizes UN court for not releasing war criminal Mladic to die at home
corpus.signal_text:
Serbia's president criticizes UN court for not releasing war criminal Mladic to die at home
BELGRADE, Serbia — Serbia's President Aleksandar Vucic on Friday accused a war crimes U.N. court in The Hague of “uncivilized behavior” for refusing to grant an early release for the former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who died Thursday at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence for his crimes.
Mladic’s family and the Serbian government had requested several times that Mladic be released, citing his age and ailing health. He died a week after the U.N. rejected his latest request for release on humanitarian grounds.
“That was uncivilized behavior, unprecedented and without excuse,” Vucic said. “We can now see that they wanted Mladic to die behind bars.”
The U.N. tribunal for war crimes committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s sentenced Mladic to life in prison in 2017 in what was considered a key step toward bringing justice to the victims. He had been in custody since 2011.
The ruthless warlord was one of the most notorious figures of the conflict that left more than 100,000 people dead and over 1 million homeless. More than three decades after the wars, former Balkan foes remain divided over his role.
In an Aug. 20 ruling, the president of the U.N. court that deals with the legacies of now-closed war crimes tribunals, Uruguayan Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, cited the “comprehensive and compassionate medical care” Mladic was receiving in custody “as well as the exceptional visitation regime allowing meaningful family contact” as reasons for turning down the request.
Bosnian Serbs held vigils and lit candles Thursday evening for Mladic, whom they consider a hero despite his conviction.
“He could not have been a better man. Everything else is just a bunch of lies. He would not touch anyone, child, no one. It's all lies,” said Stojanka Visnjevac, a resident of Kalinovik, Mladic's small hometown.
But the families of the victims of crimes Mladic orchestrated said his death means at least some justice for their loved ones.
Fazila Efendic, who lost several members of her family in the 1995 massacre of more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica, which is Europe's first acknowledged genocide since World War II, said it is important that Mladic died in prison.

corpus.title: ‘Butcher of Bosnia’ Ratko Mladic is dead — but where are the other key figures from the Balkan wars?
corpus.signal_text:
PARIS, Aug 28 — AFP looks at what became of the main players in the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, after the death of Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military leader who oversaw the 1995 Srebrenica massacre — Europe’s worst single act of bloodshed since World War II.
‘Butcher’ Mladic
Mladic, who died yesterday, was a Bosnian Serb war criminal dubbed the “Butcher of Bosnia”.
He was convicted of genocide and war crimes over the nearly-four-year siege of the Bosnian capital Sarajevo by his forces between 1992 and 1996 and the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in the town of Srebrenica in 1995, among other crimes.
He was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years on the run and transferred to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague, where he was sentenced to life imprisonment in November 2017.
The verdict against him was confirmed on appeal in 2021.
Bosnian Serb leader Karadzic
Former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic was accused of being the architect of a campaign of ethnic cleansing that saw more than a million non-Serbs driven from their homes in Bosnia alongside widespread killings and rapes.
He evaded capture for 13 years until he was arrested in 2008 on a bus in the Serbian capital Belgrade masquerading as a New Age healer.
In 2016, he was convicted in The Hague over the genocide in Srebrenica and nine other charges including extermination, deportations and hostage-taking. He was sentenced to 40 years in prison, but that was later increased to life in jail.
Yugoslav leader Milosevic
Former Serbian president and ex-Yugoslav leader Slobodan Milosevic died in his cell at The Hague in 2006, aged 64, while on trial for 66 counts including genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. An official report said he had suffered a heart attack.
He was accused of fuelling ethnic conflict and mass murder in the former Yugoslavia during his 13-year rule.
Ultranationalist Seselj
UN judges in 2018 found ultranationalist Serb politician Vojislav Seselj, arch-propagandist for a “Greater Serbia”, guilty on appeal of crimes against humanity and sentenced him to 10 years in prison.
The court said Seselj instigated the murders of scores of Croats, Muslims and other non-Serbs in incendiary speeches inciting violence against them.
As he had already spent almost 12 years in detention, the leader of the far-right Serbian Radical Party remains free.

corpus.title: Ratko Mladić is still viewed as a hero by many Bosnian Serbs. It’s a reminder how divided my country remains today
corpus.signal_text:
I was a 19-year-old living in Banja Luka, the second-largest city in Bosnia, when Yugoslavia began falling apart. What I remember most is the shock and speed with which my normal life and those of my friends abruptly ended.
At the time, I wasn’t following politics or watching the news much, so I had no idea what was to come – a full-blown war and genocide of the Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim people), led by Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serbian general and convicted war criminal, who died this week in a prison in The Hague.
Ethnicity was not something my friends and I ever talked about growing up. Two of my best friends were non-Serbs, which I only realised when they suddenly left Bosnia in April and May of 1992.
Soon after, I learned I was to be drafted into the Serbian territorial defence, not knowing what that even was. I went to pick up my uniform and boots, and that’s when my parents put me on the bus to leave the country. I didn’t know where I was going.
This was how I left my country, on my own, for the first time in my life: in haste, without goodbyes, not knowing if or when I would see my family again.
I was not the only one. Almost two million Bosnians were displaced during the war.
Now, with Mladić’s death, these memories of the war are flooding back, juxtaposed with the disheartening scenes of Mladić being celebrated by Serbs in Bosnia as a hero.
He was not a hero; nor is it helpful to refer to him simply as a “madman” or a “butcher”. Mladić is a symbolic reminder of the unresolved legacies of the war – the continued divisions among Bosnians and selective memories that many have about the atrocities that occurred.
Swift rise up the ranks
Mladić was a career military officer in the Yugoslav army. His rise through the ranks was accelerated at the beginning of the Bosnian war when he was named commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.
It’s important to understand this newly created army inherited all of its armour from the former Yugoslav army. It had all the weapons and military infrastructure in Bosnia, and was led by an experienced professional officer in Mladić.
Mladić’s army quickly took over 70% of the country, laying siege to the capital, Sarajevo. More than 100,000 people died in the war from 1992–95. At least 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by the Bosnian Serb Army in the genocide in Srebrenica in July 1995.
Mladić was the face of this ruthless military campaign, and the rise of Serb nationalism at the time.
